title: The finger and the moon
hook: a teaching points at something, so don't stare at the pointing finger (a Buddhist image, Surangama Sutra, much used in Zen)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhaozhou told a new monk: then wash your bowl. Your line was wash your bowl. Which small task did you do with your whole attention? Day forty-eight.

Try this with a very young baby. Point at a ball across the room. Often the baby looks at your finger. Grabs it, even. The ball sits there, ignored, and the baby stares at your hand, waiting for it to do something. It's sweet in a baby. It's less funny when we do it. And we do it all the time. There's a picture for this, a well-loved one in the Buddhist world, and Zen teachers have used it for many centuries. Someone points at the moon. And the other person looks at the finger. Today's story is the finger and the moon.
screen: `POINT AT THE BALL.` → `THE BABY LOOKS AT YOUR FINGER.` → `SOMEONE POINTS AT THE MOON.`

segments.voice: The picture appears in a Mahayana Buddhist scripture called the Surangama Sutra. The Buddha is talking with his cousin and attendant Ananda, who has heard a great many teachings and remembers every word. And the Buddha tells him, more or less: when someone points at the moon to show it to you, you should follow the finger and look at the moon. If you look at the finger and take it for the moon, you lose the moon. And you lose the finger too, because you've mistaken what a finger is for. That last part is sharp. It's not just that you miss the moon. You also misunderstand the pointing. A finger is for looking past. Zen took this image and ran with it. A famous old story tells of the teacher Huineng, who couldn't read, being asked by a nun how he could understand scriptures he couldn't even read. And he answers with this picture: the truth is like the moon, and words are like a finger. You can see the moon without the finger. Here's why it matters beyond Zen. Every teaching points. Words, books, rituals, even these lessons. They're fingers. They are precious, and worth studying, and they are not the thing. The danger is falling in love with the pointing: memorizing the words, arguing about the finger's shape, collecting fingers. And missing the moon, which is right there, and was the point. So when you hear a teaching, ask: what is this pointing at? Then look there.
screen: `THE SURANGAMA SUTRA.` · `YOU LOSE THE MOON AND THE FINGER.` · `HUINENG: WORDS ARE THE FINGER.` · `WHAT IS THIS POINTING AT?` · then, large: `NOT THE FINGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the sky, not the screen. When the bell starts, put this phone face down, and if you can, go to a window or step outside. Look up. Whatever's there: clouds, blue, gray, the moon if you're lucky, a ceiling if that's all there is. This lesson was the finger. The sky is the moon. Just look. Let it be bigger than anything you've read today. The bell holds the time.
The finger and the moon. Teachings point beyond themselves; don't stare at the finger and miss the moon. Today's word.
screen: `THE FINGER AND THE MOON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not the finger. Today, when you catch yourself arguing over the words, stop and ask what they were pointing at. Then look there. Day forty-eight.

howItsDone: Zen teachers often use the finger and the moon to remind students that sutras, koans and talks point toward direct experience, and many Zen schools pair careful study with sitting practice for that reason.

fork.setup: someone points at the moon to show it to you. where do you look?
options: along the finger, at the moon.
fork.reveal: follow the finger to the moon. take the finger for the moon, the sutra says, and you lose both.

original.note: Chinese, zhǐ yuè: pointing at the moon, the short name Chinese Buddhism uses for this image.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be distracted by someone's hand.
what it means: teachings point beyond themselves; if you stare at the words, you miss what they were for.
what a scholar hears: Surangama Sutra, the Buddha to Ananda: mistake the finger for the moon and you lose both. Zen tells a version of Huineng with it.

sources.ref: Surangama Sutra, fascicle 2 (the finger pointing at the moon)

notes: Surangama Sutra passage (fascicle 2) paraphrased; no public-domain English translation is on the approved list. Confirm the 'lose both the moon and the finger' reading. The sutra's Indian origin is debated (many scholars think it was composed in China); not raised in the script. A Buddhist Keeper may want it mentioned.
Ananda described as the Buddha's cousin and attendant who remembered every teaching: confirm.
Huineng and the nun Wujinzang: this story appears in later Chan sources, not in the Platform Sutra itself; told as 'a famous old story'. Confirm.
The baby-and-pointing hook: very young infants often look at the hand rather than the target; following a point develops around 9–12 months. Worded as 'often'.

Reviewer edit: the hook originally called this 'one of the oldest' Buddhist images used 'for over a thousand years'. Softened to 'a well-loved one' used 'for many centuries', since the Surangama Sutra's date and origin are debated. The image also appears in the Lankavatara Sutra; a Keeper may prefer to mention it.
